summary: This topic introduces client-side programmability using JavaScript (ECMAScript) to transform static HTML/CSS documents into responsive, interactive web applications. The language foundations contrast block-scoped `let` and `const` against legacy function-scoped `var`, and detail strict equality (`===`) versus loose type-coercing equality (`==`). The Document Object Model (DOM) represents the webpage in memory as a live object tree of nodes. Students master DOM selection (`getElementById`, `querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`), content modification (`textContent` for safe plain text versus `innerHTML` with its Cross-Site Scripting [XSS] vulnerabilities), and attribute/class manipulation via the `classList` API. Finally, the topic analyzes the browser event model: attaching event listeners with `addEventListener`, managing default behaviors with `event.preventDefault()`, and harnessing event bubbling for high-performance Event Delegation.

key_terms.definition: A programming interface and object-oriented tree representation of an HTML document constructed by the browser engine, allowing scripts to dynamically inspect and modify elements, attributes, and styles.
The identity comparison operator in JavaScript that checks whether two operands have both the same value AND the same data type without performing implicit type coercion.

A method of the Event interface that cancels the default action of the browser that belongs to the event (such as preventing a form from submitting and reloading the page).
A design pattern where a single event listener is attached to a parent element to manage events triggered by existing or dynamically added child elements, leveraging event bubbling.
'textContent' safely sets or gets the raw unparsed text content of a node, whereas 'innerHTML' parses strings as HTML markup, exposing applications to XSS vulnerabilities if user input is unescaped.
A DOM property offering convenient methods (add, remove, toggle, contains) to manipulate the class attribute of an element cleanly without string concatenation.
ES6 variable declarations: 'let' declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned; 'const' declares a block-scoped variable whose identifier binding cannot be reassigned.

questions.explanation: In JavaScript, the loose equality operator `==` performs implicit type coercion: it converts the string `'5'` to the number `5` before comparison, returning `true`. In contrast, the strict equality operator `===` checks both value and data type without coercion; because `number` does not equal `string`, it returns `false`.

questions.question: In modern ECMAScript (ES6+), why is declaring variables with `let` and `const` vastly preferred over the legacy keyword `var`?
options: `var` can only be used on Linux servers
`let` and `const` are block-scoped `{ }`, preventing accidental variable leaking and bugs caused by `var`'s function scoping and confusing variable hoisting behavior
`const` variables can be reassigned infinite times, while `var` cannot
`let` and `const` automatically compile to C programming binaries
questions.explanation: `var` is function-scoped (or global if outside a function) and is hoisted to the top of its scope initialized as `undefined`, which frequently causes subtle scoping bugs in loops and conditionals. `let` and `const` are strictly block-scoped to the enclosing curly braces `{ }` and enforce the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ), throwing clear ReferenceErrors if accessed before declaration.

why_wrong.0: `var` is standard JavaScript supported on all operating systems.
why_wrong.2: `const` variables CANNOT be reassigned; that is their defining property.
why_wrong.3: JavaScript variables execute in browser JS engines (V8, SpiderMonkey), not compiled to C binaries.

questions.source: IFT 203 Syllabus; MDN let and const

questions.question: A developer needs to select ALL student cards on a page with the class `.student-card` to loop through them and attach an event listener. Which DOM method should be used, and what does it return?
options: `document.getElementById('.student-card')` returning an array
`document.querySelector('.student-card')` returning a single Element node
`document.querySelectorAll('.student-card')` returning a static `NodeList` of all matching elements
`document.getElementsByTagName('.student-card')` returning a JSON string
questions.explanation: `document.querySelectorAll()` takes any valid CSS selector string and returns a static `NodeList` containing all matching element nodes in the DOM, which can be directly iterated over using `.forEach()`. `querySelector()` returns only the *first* matching element. `getElementById()` only matches IDs and takes raw ID names without dots.

why_wrong.0: `getElementById` expects an ID name without a dot, and returns a single element, not an array.
why_wrong.1: `querySelector` stops after finding the first matching element, failing to select all cards.
why_wrong.3: `getElementsByTagName` expects HTML tag names (e.g., `'div'`), not class selectors with dots.

questions.question: Which of the following are standard, built-in JavaScript DOM events frequently used in web application development? (Select ALL that apply)
options: `DOMContentLoaded`: Fires when the initial HTML document has been completely parsed without waiting for stylesheets and images to finish loading
`submit`: Fires when an HTML `<form>` is submitted by clicking a submit button or pressing Enter in an input field
`input`: Fires synchronously every time the value of an `<input>`, `<select>`, or `<textarea>` element is changed by the user
`compile`: Fires when the browser compiles HTML into C language binary code
questions.explanation: `DOMContentLoaded`, `submit`, and `input` are foundational W3C DOM events. There is no `compile` event in web browsers; HTML and JS are interpreted/JIT-compiled by the browser engine without converting to C binaries.

why_wrong.3: `compile` is not a DOM event; HTML is markup parsed by browsers, not compiled into C binaries.

questions.question: What is the specific role of JavaScript in the 'Web Triumvirate' (HTML, CSS, JavaScript)?
questions.answer: HTML defines the structure/content, CSS defines the presentation/styling, and JavaScript defines dynamic behavior, logic, and client-side user interactivity.
questions.explanation: Core web technology triad taught across all university curricula.

questions.question: Compare `let`, `const`, and `var` in JavaScript scoping and reassignment.
questions.answer:
- `var`: Function-scoped, hoisted to top with undefined, reassignable.
- `let`: Block-scoped `{ }`, not hoisted before declaration (TDZ), reassignable.
- `const`: Block-scoped `{ }`, cannot be reassigned (immutable identifier binding).
questions.explanation: In modern ECMAScript (ES6+): 'var' is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined initialization (prone to bugs); 'let' is block-scoped, not accessible before declaration (Temporal Dead Zone), and allows reassignment; 'const' is block-scoped, cannot be reassigned after declaration, and requires immediate initialization. (MDN JavaScript Reference).

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?
questions.answer: `==` (loose equality) compares values after converting them to a common type (type coercion). `===` (strict equality) compares BOTH value and data type without coercion.
questions.explanation: Always use `===` in production JavaScript to prevent unexpected type coercion bugs.

questions.question: What is the Document Object Model (DOM)?
questions.answer: A tree-structured in-memory object representation of an HTML document created by the browser engine upon loading, providing an API for JavaScript to access and modify page content and styles.
questions.explanation: The Document Object Model (DOM) is a cross-platform, language-independent W3C programming interface that represents HTML and XML documents as a hierarchical tree of objects and nodes, allowing programming languages (such as JavaScript) to dynamically inspect, modify, add, or delete document content, structure, and styles. (W3C DOM Level 4).

questions.question: How does `document.querySelector()` differ from `document.querySelectorAll()`?
questions.answer:
`querySelector()` returns only the FIRST element that matches the specified CSS selector string.
`querySelectorAll()` returns a static `NodeList` containing ALL elements that match the selector.
questions.explanation: The method 'document.querySelector(selector)' returns the first Element within the document that matches the specified CSS selector, or null if no match is found. In contrast, 'document.querySelectorAll(selector)' returns a static NodeList representing all matching elements in document order. (W3C Selectors API).

questions.question: Why is `element.textContent` preferred over `element.innerHTML` for inserting user text?
questions.answer: `textContent` treats all strings as raw plain text, preventing Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. `innerHTML` parses tags and can execute injected malicious `
questions.explanation: Assigning unvalidated user input to 'element.innerHTML' parses strings as executable HTML markup, exposing the application to catastrophic Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. Using 'element.textContent' ensures the browser treats data strictly as raw literal text, automatically neutralizing malicious script injection tags. (OWASP Top 10: XSS Prevention).

questions.question: What does `event.preventDefault()` do in an event handler?
questions.answer: It stops the browser from executing the native default action associated with that event (e.g., stopping a form from reloading the page upon submission, or stopping an anchor link from navigating).
questions.explanation: Indispensable method for single-page applications and AJAX validation.

questions.question: What is Event Delegation, and why is it efficient?
questions.answer: Attaching a single event listener to a common parent element rather than attaching separate listeners to dozens of child elements. It saves memory and automatically handles dynamically added child elements via event bubbling.
questions.explanation: Event Delegation is a high-performance DOM event handling design pattern where a single event listener is attached to a common ancestor element rather than attaching individual listeners to multiple child elements. It leverages the DOM Event Bubbling phase ('event.target') to handle clicks on current and dynamically added children with minimal memory overhead. (MDN Event Reference).

case_studies.scenario: A departmental portal displays a dynamic list of 40 available Nile University elective courses. Students can click an 'Add Course' button next to any course to append it to their Registered Courses list, updating their Total Credit Units counter. A junior developer writes a `for` loop that queries all 40 buttons and attaches an individual `addEventListener('click')` to each button. When a new course is dynamically loaded via an AJAX fetch, clicking its 'Add Course' button does nothing.

sub_questions.question: Why did clicking the newly added course button fail, and what design pattern permanently solves this problem while using significantly less browser memory?
options: Buttons can only be clicked once in their lifetime

The newly added button was created after the initial `for` loop finished executing, so it has no listener attached. The solution is 'Event Delegation': attaching a single listener to the parent container (`<ul>`) and inspecting `event.target` using event bubbling
The browser memory was exhausted by JavaScript
Event listeners only work on Tuesday mornings
sub_questions.explanation: Attaching listeners in a loop binds handlers only to elements currently in the DOM at execution time; dynamically inserted elements remain unhandled. Furthermore, creating 40+ separate listener functions wastes memory. Event Delegation attaches ONE listener to the parent container: when a child button is clicked, the click event bubbles up to the parent, which checks `if (event.target.classList.contains('add-btn'))`, seamlessly handling present and future dynamic elements.

why_wrong.0: Buttons can be clicked unlimited times unless explicitly disabled.
why_wrong.2: 40 listeners consumes memory unnecessarily, but does not crash the browser completely.

sub_questions.source: MDN Event Delegation; High Performance JavaScript
